snip.t: | Chronic compartment syndrome | Severe exertional calf pain in young athletes or soldiers | Normal pulses; elevated intra-compartmental pressures after exercise |
Neurological status – sensory loss may indicate compartment syndrome or nerve involvement.
Local: abscess formation, ulceration, chronic sinus tract, lymphangitis, compartment syndrome.
Neurovascular status – intact distal pulses, sensation: Needed to rule out compartment syndrome or vascular compromise secondary to swelling.

Compartments: the leg (anterior, lateral, superficial posterior and deep posterior), the forearm (volar/flexor and dorsal/extensor), thigh, hand, foot, buttock, and abdomen (abdominal compartment syndrome).

qs.q: Which of the following clinical scenarios represents the single most common cause of acute compartment syndrome in orthopaedic trauma?
o: Simple distal radius fracture in an elderly patient
qs.e: Fractures—specifically tibial shaft, supracondylar humerus, and forearm fractures—are listed as the commonest causes of acute compartment syndrome. Tibial shaft fractures carry particularly high risk among long bone injuries.

qs.q: A 45-year-old man undergoes successful emergency revascularization for an acute lower‑limb arterial embolus. Two hours later his calf becomes tense and painful. Which mechanism most commonly precipitates compartment syndrome in this reperfusion setting?
o: Reperfusion-induced capillary leak and tissue edema
Embolic material obstructing the deep peroneal veins
Mechanical compression from surgical clamp placement
Thrombosis of the proximal collateral arterial network
qs.e: Reperfusion injury increases capillary permeability, leading to tissue edema that raises compartment pressure. The other options involve vascular obstruction or external compression, which are not typical after restoration of blood flow.
